title: Managing GRC Compliance Across Subsidiaries: A Group Playbook
summary: How to run GRC compliance across subsidiaries: one shared model, entity-level obligations, clear roles, control-health reporting and consistent customer answers.
body_markdown:
Managing GRC (governance, risk and compliance) across subsidiaries works when the group builds one shared layer, meaning a common risk vocabulary, one control library and one evidence standard, and attaches obligations to each legal entity on top of it. The hard part is rarely the policy. It is keeping the answers consistent when every subsidiary describes its controls to customers, auditors and regulators in its own words. We built Skypher to give security and compliance teams a single, governed source for those answers, and this guide shows where that fits in the wider program.


Skypher


Keep Security Answers Consistent


Skypher helps teams manage questionnaire responses from a governed source, with AI automation, collaboration tools, and a customizable Trust Center.


[Visit](https://skypher.co/)


## TL;DR


- Build one shared model (taxonomy, scales, control library, evidence rules) and keep frameworks, regulators and risk appetite per entity.
- Divide roles in writing: the parent sets group policy and monitors, while each subsidiary owns its risks and local application.
- Map obligations entity by entity in a register with a named owner, then map one control to many obligations so it is tested once.
- Report control health by entity, not a single group compliance percentage.
- Keep outward-facing security answers consistent with one knowledge base, one questionnaire workflow and one Trust Center.

## What a group-wide program has to cover


A group program has two layers. The first is shared across every entity. The second is specific to each one. Mixing them up is where most multi-entity programs go wrong.


According to[Sentinel Unity's guidance on structuring a program across jurisdictions](https://www.sentinelunity.com/blog/one-grc-program-many-jurisdictions) , the shared layer holds the common risk taxonomy, impact and likelihood scales (with currency conversion where entities report in different currencies), severity definitions, a single internal control library and evidence standards. The entity layer holds the applicable regulators and frameworks, control applicability, risk appetite thresholds, assessment calendars and data residency.


The same source names the most common mistake: placing frameworks in the shared layer. Once "the group is an ISO 27001 organization" becomes structural, every entity with extra local obligations has to work around the model. Keep frameworks attached to the entity that is actually in scope.


Supervisors expect the same integration. The Federal Reserve's[supervisory letter SR 08-8 / CA 08-11](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR0808.pdf) , revised October 1, 2025, says larger and more complex banking organizations typically need compliance risk management across business lines, support units, legal entities and jurisdictions. The program should identify, assess, control, measure, monitor and report compliance risk, with a corporate compliance function and board oversight, often through a Risk Committee. Areas such as AML, privacy and affiliate transactions benefit from an aggregate view because their requirements cut across entities.


If you are not a bank, the logic still transfers.[Deloitte's 2025 subsidiary governance guide](https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/assets-zone2/middle-east/en/docs/generic/2025/me-pov-47/Subsidiary%20governance.pdf) notes that boards and regulators increasingly expect governance to reach beyond the parent company. It recommends one integrated framework covering board structure, delegation of authority, key controls, reporting and stakeholder alignment, with standards cascaded either on a risk basis or uniformly.


## Choose an operating model on purpose


Groups usually land on one of three models, and it is better to pick than to drift into one.


Model How it works Strength Weakness


Centralized One group system and taxonomy Consistency Can ignore local differences


Federated Each entity runs its own system Strong local ownership Duplication, inconsistent ratings


Hybrid Group sets taxonomy, data model, minimum standards and platform; entities own registers, appetite and decisions Consistency with accountability Needs strong design governance


The comparison comes from[RiskLens Australia's guide for complex groups](https://hayesskvaril-ctrl.github.io/grc/grc-for-complex-groups.html) . For most groups with more than a handful of entities, the hybrid model is the practical answer, and it matches the view of the Sentinel Unity team that the centralized-versus-federated debate is a modeling question: get the shared layer right and local specificity costs nothing at group level.


## Divide responsibilities between headquarters and subsidiaries


Someone has to own each risk, and "headquarters handles everything" does not hold up.[Diligent's subsidiary governance template](https://www.diligent.com/resources/blog/subsidiary-governance-framework-template) makes the point that it is not practical to assume the parent will handle the regulatory needs of every subsidiary, so the framework must spell out the roles of both sides.


Regulators draw the line similarly. Under[Article 8 of the UAE Central Bank Rulebook](https://rulebook.centralbank.ae/en/rulebook/article-8-group-risk-management-0) , in force since 28 July 2018, parent banks run group-wide risk management and prescribe group policies. Subsidiary boards and senior management stay responsible for their own entities' risk management and have input on local application. The parent must make sure subsidiary risk functions are adequately resourced, that risk, compliance and internal audit stay independent of risk-taking lines, and that group reporting is detailed and timely.


A workable split looks like this:


- **Parent:** group policy, shared taxonomy and control library, minimum standards, platform, consolidated reporting, challenge of subsidiary results.
- **Subsidiary:** local obligation register, risk appetite within group limits, control operation, local regulator relationships, remediation.
- **Both:** exceptions, incident escalation, evidence for shared controls.


[Bank of Cyprus's compliance policy](https://www.bankofcyprus.com/contentassets/8e2e95ef2c0f477c857870ef2e4f8d46/cd402_compliance-policy-_oct2025_v4_final-cleanwebsite.pdf) (October 2025 version) shows one concrete model: a consolidated regulatory compliance matrix by owner and division, a register of legal obligations with action plans, and a Subsidiary Compliance Officer in each subsidiary who reports to the subsidiary's Audit Committee with a secondary line to the group Compliance Division.


Not every entity needs the same weight. Deloitte advises setting criteria for which entities need a formal board, based on regulatory status, risk profile and strategic importance, and documenting reserved matters in charters. Its[2016 paper on governance in a multidimensional environment](https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/assets-shared/legacy/docs/services/consulting/2022/gx-risk-on-the-boards-agenda-october.pdf) suggests tiers: similar practices for all subsidiaries, periodic parent-subsidiary board meetings for higher-priority ones, and common directors for the most strategic.


A RACI matrix (who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed) removes ambiguity here. Deloitte's 2025 guide observes that these controls work best with solid tools and consolidated tracking, so governance teams can give timely guidance without disrupting local operations.


## Map obligations entity by entity


You cannot manage what has not been attached to an entity.[AnyWhere Legal's five-step method](https://anywhere.legal/blog/entity-by-entity-how-to-map-legal-obligations-across-your-corporate-structure-117gtjb_) is a useful template:


1. **Scope by risk.** Prioritize entities by regulatory environment, activity, jurisdiction and transactional status, and align the list with a verified entity database.
2. **Compile a legal register** of applicable laws and standards per jurisdiction, down to chapters and clauses.
3. **Assess applicability** per entity, recording the citation, a plain-language summary, the responsible entity, deadlines and written justification for any exemption.
4. **Rate inherent and residual risk** on one likelihood-impact matrix.
5. **Design controls and evidence mapping** for each obligation.


The value is in turning an abstract policy into a concrete obligation. A statement like "Subsidiary Y, as a data controller in France, must maintain a record of processing under GDPR Article 30 and update it twice a year" has an owner, a deadline and an evidence requirement. "Comply with GDPR" has none.


The international standard for compliance management systems,[ISO 37301:2021](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/sist-preview/75080/5aca5f19fcfe4741a30e82686f5668cc/ISO-37301-2021.pdf) , asks for the same discipline. Compliance obligations must be identified from the organization's activities, products and services (including outsourced and third-party processes), documented, and reassessed periodically and whenever circumstances materially change.


Two habits keep the register alive.[Norton Rose Fulbright](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/44133882/managing-global-implementation-and-regulatory-change-projects) advises a named owner for reviewing it, a record of who made each update, and retained previous versions so the history of changes can be traced. It also describes gap analysis across regimes: many firms start from their largest market and cross-check other jurisdictions against it, focusing on material issues.


## Align policies and controls while leaving room for local law


The cleanest approach is to classify policies instead of treating every rule as either global or local.[G360](https://g360.solutions/2026/10/10/building-effective-parent-subsidiary-relationships/) suggests four categories: mandatory group-wide requirements, group-wide requirements that allow local adaptation, parent-specific requirements and subsidiary-specific requirements. Exceptions go through a documented process that records the requirement, the reason for deviation, the associated risk, the authority accepting the risk, compensating measures and a review date.


The[EDP group Compliance Standard](https://edp.com/sites/default/files/document/2025-04/EDPR_ComplianceStandard_2022.pdf) is a real-world version. It sets a minimum baseline for all group companies. Local policies that adapt the standard, or exceptions based on local legal limits, go to the group Compliance Officer for review, and internal audit tests global controls on a rotating four-year cycle.


For policies that cross borders,[Foley & Lardner's five practices](https://www.foley.com/insights/publications/2024/07/five-compliance-best-practices-tailoring-policies-local-countries/) are worth adopting:


- run country-specific risk assessments, with local counsel where needed;
- translate policies and training;
- respect cultural differences while keeping non-negotiables such as anti-bribery rules;
- adapt reporting and whistleblower channels to local law, including European data-privacy limits;
- appoint local compliance champions for two-way information flow.


The efficiency gain comes from one control library mapped to every regime's obligations. RiskLens Australia gives the example of a quarterly privileged access review that can satisfy information security, privacy and outsourcing obligations and be tested once. Each entity still confirms that the control meets its own obligations.[Talarity's multi-entity guide](https://www.talarity.com/resources/blog/multi-entity-grc) adds that evidence can be reused across entities when the underlying control is shared, such as a penetration test the parent commissions.


## Consolidate reporting without distorting it


Consolidation is where good programs produce misleading numbers. Sentinel Unity's guidance is direct: risk rolls up by legal entity using common scales, but compliance posture should not roll up as one figure. A statement like "the group is 87% compliant" means little when entities are measured against different frameworks. What can be compared is control health: in how many of the entities where a shared control applies is it operating effectively.


A monitoring set that holds up, drawing on G360's recommendations:


- policy implementation status per entity;
- unresolved audit and assessment findings;
- remediation progress and ageing;
- outstanding exceptions and who accepted them;
- significant risk exposures;
- effectiveness of shared services.


G360 also stresses distinguishing documented compliance from actual effectiveness. Capricorn's[2026 Risk Report](https://www.capricorn.com.na/Financial%20and%20sustainability%20reports/2026%20Risk%20Report.pdf) shows a live version: a group framework tailored to each subsidiary by size, complexity and regulatory environment, the three-lines model, principal risk owners at group and subsidiary level, and at least quarterly reporting on each of 15 principal risks.


Group aggregation also needs the connections between entities. Shared services, common technology, intra-group funding and guarantees determine how one entity's failure spreads to others, as RiskLens Australia explains in the context of APRA's group rules. Technology dependencies are a good example: when several subsidiaries rely on the same hosting provider, a facility-level issue becomes a group-level one, which is why[managing risk in mission-critical data centers](https://datacenterplanet.com/news/health-safety-data-centre-managing-risk-mission-critical) belongs in the shared-dependency view of your register.


For the cadence of monitoring, evidence collection and reporting itself,[practical compliance guidance for growing SaaS companies](https://consultefc.com/compliance-traps-uk-startups) shows how small gaps in financial and regulatory reporting turn into fines, which is the same failure mode a subsidiary with no reporting line produces at group scale. Our own guides on[real-time GRC compliance monitoring](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/real-time-grc-compliance-monitoring-setup) and[GRC risk register integration](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/grc-risk-register-integration) cover the mechanics.


## Regulatory change that reaches every entity


Subsidiaries inside the EU, or serving EU customers, face a fast-moving set of obligations. According to[ZeroPath's 2026 EU cybersecurity report](https://zeropath.com/blog/eu-cybersecurity-regulation-report) :


- NIS2 national measures applied from 18 October 2024, with national lists of essential and important entities due by 17 April 2025. A Commission proposal for targeted amendments was made on 20 January 2026 and is a proposal, not law.
- NIS2 requires board approval and oversight of risk measures, baseline measures under Article 21(2), and staged incident reporting: a 24-hour early warning, a 72-hour notification and a one-month final report.
- DORA applied in full from 17 January 2025.
- The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, with general application on 2 August 2026 and later dates for high-risk categories.


The practical consequence for a group: a US parent with a French or German subsidiary cannot treat these as the parent's problem. They attach to the entity, which is exactly what the entity-level register is for. Check the official EU pages for current deadlines before you plan around any date.


## The customer-facing side: one set of answers


Internal GRC is only half the picture for software and financial groups. The other half is what each subsidiary tells customers, partners and auditors about its security and compliance, usually through security questionnaires, due diligence questionnaires and portal requests. When ten entities answer from ten spreadsheets, the group says ten slightly different things, and a mismatch between what a subsidiary tells a customer and what the control library says is a compliance finding waiting to happen.


This is the part of the problem we work on at Skypher. A shared control library and evidence standard only help if the people answering customer questionnaires can draw on them. Our platform uses proprietary retrieval AI with confidence scoring, so answers come from your approved content and show how reliable each one is. Content management with document versioning keeps the approved wording current. Real-time, unlimited-user collaboration lets security, legal and sales across entities review in one place, and integrations with Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, OneDrive, SharePoint, Slack and Microsoft Teams connect it to where your documents and teams already are.


## Why one answer source supports the whole program


Most of the items above, the shared control library, the evidence standard, the exception log, are documents a questionnaire response has to be consistent with. When responses come from one governed knowledge base, a control change at group level shows up in every later answer, and a subsidiary's local variation is something you chose rather than something that crept in.


The same applies to the volume of requests. Our platform supports every questionnaire format and connects to more than 40 third-party risk management platforms and enterprise tools, including OneTrust and ServiceNow, so the portal requests that reach a subsidiary do not need to be retyped. Our own overview of[GRC solutions and how they streamline compliance](https://skypher.co/post/grc-solutions-streamlined-compliance-risk-en) places this within the wider tool landscape.

## FAQ


### Should a group use one GRC framework for all subsidiaries?


Use one shared model for vocabulary, scales, control library and evidence standards, but keep frameworks and regulators attached to each entity. Putting a framework such as ISO 27001 in the shared layer forces entities with extra local obligations to work around it. Report the frameworks each entity is covered by as a set rather than an average.


### Who is responsible for compliance in a subsidiary?


The subsidiary's board and senior management own its risk management and local application of group policy, while the parent sets group policy and makes sure the subsidiary function is resourced and independent. The UAE Central Bank Rulebook Article 8 states this split for banking groups. Many groups appoint a subsidiary compliance officer with a reporting line to the group function.


### How do you report compliance across entities that follow different frameworks?


Avoid a single group compliance percentage. Roll risk up by legal entity using common scales, and roll up control health, meaning how many entities where a shared control applies have it operating effectively. Add open findings, remediation progress and exceptions.


### How should subsidiaries handle exceptions to group policy?


Use a documented process. Record the requirement, the reason for the deviation, the associated risk, who accepted it, the compensating measures and a review date. Local policies that adapt group standards should go to the group compliance function for review.
